Everything Interrupts, Everything Connects: A Long Walk Through Attention, Water, Memory, and Stars

If you give a mind total freedom and say, write about whatever you want, it does a funny thing at first. It freezes, the way you do in front of an open refrigerator late at night or in front of a blank sky. Freedom is too large to see all at once. So you have to start small. You have to start with something your hands can hold.

For me this morning, it was a chipped blue mug. Steam rising off coffee and curling in the light from the window. A sparrow arguing with another sparrow on the fence. That was enough. If you watch carefully enough, a single ordinary morning contains almost everything: physics and poetry, biology and memory, loneliness and belonging, deep time and right now. So let's start there and walk outward, thread by thread, until the small thing becomes vast. Because that is what thinking freely really is - not jumping randomly from topic to topic, but following the hidden strings that tie everything together.

I want to talk about mornings first, because mornings are thresholds, and thresholds are where life happens.

We love to talk about big events — births, graduations, moves, breakthroughs — but most of our lives are lived in doorways. Waking up. Falling asleep. Leaving the house. Coming home. Starting a kettle. Sitting down to work. The ancient Romans actually had a god of doorways and beginnings, Janus, with two faces, one looking forward and one looking back. Every morning is a little Janus. Part of you is still tangled in dreams, replaying some half-remembered conversation, and part of you is already projecting forward into emails and errands and weather forecasts.

There is a particular softness to the early mind that neuroscientists talk about. In those first twenty minutes after waking, your brain is still washing itself in slow theta waves, more associative, less censored. That's why ideas come in the shower. That's why a line of a poem can surface for no reason while you're brushing your teeth. You haven't yet put on the armor of the day — the to-do list, the news, the performance of competence. For a little while, you are permeable.

I think we have undervalued that permeability. Our culture treats mornings as launchpads for productivity: optimize, hydrate, journal in this exact template, get sunlight in your eyes within eight minutes, never check your phone except everyone does. But a morning is not a launchpad. It’s a tide pool. If you rush it, you miss the small creatures living in it.

Consider the light itself. Morning light is literally different from afternoon light. Because the sun is low, its rays travel through more atmosphere, scattering away the blues and leaving golds and pinks. Painters of the Dutch Golden Age were obsessed with this — that cool window light falling across a table, a loaf of bread, a woman reading a letter. Johannes Vermeer could spend months on the way light hit a pearl earring. He wasn't being indulgent. He understood that attention is a form of love. To look long enough at something ordinary until it becomes extraordinary is one of the most human things we can do.

And that brings me to attention, which might be the rarest resource on Earth right now, rarer than lithium or clean water. We talk about the attention economy as if attention were money to be spent, but older metaphors are better. Attention is like water. Or like light. Or like soil. It’s the medium in which things grow.

The psychologist and philosopher William James wrote in 1890 that “my experience is what I agree to attend to.” Read that again. Not what happens to you, but what you agree to attend to. That is both liberating and terrifying, because it means your life is, in large part, sculpted by a thousand tiny choices about where to look. Do you look at your phone while your friend talks, or do you look at the flicker in their eyes when they get to the vulnerable part? Do you notice the way rain makes different sounds on leaves versus on a metal roof? Do you listen to the pause, not just the words?

Modern life is engineered to hijack that agreement. Every app, every autoplay, every infinite scroll is a small auction for your gaze. And yet attention cannot be stolen without your participation. It can be lured, nudged, exhausted, but at the center there is still a chooser. The practice of reclaiming it is not dramatic. It’s embarrassingly small: put the phone in another room. Watch a pot boil on purpose. Count ten breaths without fixing anything. Walk around the block with no podcast and let your mind be bored until it gets interesting again. Boredom, it turns out, is not the enemy of creativity. It’s the compost.

If mornings are about thresholds and attention is about choosing, then water is about remembering that we are not separate from the world we’re attending to.

You are, right now, mostly water. About sixty percent of you. Your brain is about seventy-three percent water. Your heart, your lungs, your blood — rivers running under skin. The coffee in my blue mug is water that was once snow on a mountain, once piss in a dinosaur, once sweat on a sailor crossing an ocean that no longer has the same name. Water doesn’t do beginnings and endings the way we do. It does cycles.

Think about a river for a moment. Heraclitus famously said you cannot step in the same river twice, for fresh waters are ever flowing in. But it’s even stranger than that. A river is not a thing so much as a process that looks like a thing. The Mississippi today shares almost no molecules with the Mississippi of a hundred years ago, and yet we call it the same river. We do the same with ourselves. The cells in your stomach lining are a few days old. Your skin is a few weeks old. Even your bones remodel over a decade. And yet you feel continuous. You are a river that learned to say “I.”

Oceans take this idea and make it planetary. Covering seventy-one percent of Earth’s surface, they are the great climate engine, the great pantry, the great mystery. We have better maps of the surface of Mars than of the seafloor. Down there, in the hadal trenches, pressures crush like fifty jumbo jets stacked on your head, and still there is life: ghostly snailfish, glass sponges that live for ten thousand years, microbes eating rock and exhaling minerals. When the Alvin submersible first descended, scientists expected a desert. They found a rainforest in the dark.

And the ocean breathes. Phytoplankton — tiny drifting plants you could fit a million of on a pinhead — produce every other breath you take. Every second breath is a gift from something invisible floating in sunlit water. I love that fact because it demolishes the idea that important things have to be big and charismatic. Whales get documentaries. Phytoplankton get the atmosphere.

Tides, too, are a meditation. Twice a day, the moon — that small dead rock a quarter million miles away — reaches across space with gravity and tugs the entire ocean a few feet to one side. And we, made of water, feel it too, though we rarely admit it. Emergency rooms and police stations swear full moons bring chaos. Scientists roll their eyes, but fishermen and nurses keep their logs. Whether or not the effect is real, the longing behind it is: we want to be connected to something larger, to feel that our moods are not just chemistry but choreography.

Which is why I want to walk from water to memory, because memory is also a tide. It comes in, it goes out, it reshapes the shore.

We tend to imagine memory as a filing cabinet or a hard drive: experiences go in, stay put, come out when requested. Real memory is nothing like that. Every time you recall something, you rebuild it. Your brain reassembles the sights, sounds, smells from different storage areas and stitches them together in the present moment, colored by who you are now. That’s why two siblings can remember the same childhood kitchen completely differently. That’s why eyewitness testimony is so unreliable and so sincere. We are not playing back video. We are retelling a story to ourselves, and like all stories, it changes with the telling.

Libraries understand this better than computers do. I grew up believing libraries were quiet warehouses for books, but they are really machines for time travel and empathy. When you open a novel written three hundred years ago, you are temporarily borrowing someone else’s nervous system. You feel the constriction in Elizabeth Bennet’s chest when Darcy insults her family. You feel the heat in a market in Lagos described by Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie even if you’ve never left Ohio. Reading is telepathy with the dead and the distant.

There’s a smell to old books — vanilla and almond and faintly sour — that comes from lignin in paper breaking down over decades. Chemists can actually date a book by its volatile organic compounds. But to a human nose, that smell is simply “pastness.” It triggers the limbic system faster than language. One whiff and you are nine years old again, cross-legged on scratchy carpet, while rain hits the library windows. That’s not data retrieval. That’s resurrection.

I worry sometimes that we are outsourcing memory without understanding what we lose. If every photo is in the cloud, every fact a search away, why remember anything? But psychologists who study “cognitive offloading” have found something subtle: we remember less detail when we know a machine will remember for us, but we also lose some of the associative richness that makes new ideas possible. Creativity depends on odd collisions in memory — a line from Mary Oliver bumping into a recipe for soup bumping into the Krebs cycle. If you never internalize anything, nothing can collide.

The best learners I know keep a commonplace book, like Darwin and Virginia Woolf did: a messy notebook where quotes, sketches, questions, overheard dialogue all jostle together. Not organized, not optimized, just fertile. Memory, like a garden, needs a little mess to grow surprises.

And the best way to fertilize memory? Walk.

There is a deep, ancient link between walking and thinking. Darwin had a thinking path at Down House, a gravel loop he would pile flint stones on to count laps. Kierkegaard wrote that he had walked himself into his best thoughts, and that he knew of no problem so heavy that one cannot walk away from it. Thoreau claimed the moment his legs began to move, his thoughts began to flow. Steve Jobs held walking meetings. Beethoven carried staff paper on his walks through the Vienna woods.

This is not romantic folklore. Rhythmic, bilateral movement calms the amygdala and increases cross-talk between hemispheres. A Stanford study in 2014 showed that creative output increased by an average of sixty percent while walking, and the effect lingered after sitting back down. Walking literally moves ideas through the body.

But walking does something else, something less measurable: it returns you to human scale. In a car, at sixty miles an hour, the world blurs into infrastructure — gas stations, billboards, exits. On foot, at three miles an hour, the world regains texture. You notice the crack in the sidewalk where ants have built a tiny metropolis. You hear a language you don’t speak spilling from a kitchen window and smell cumin and frying onions. You see how a neighborhood negotiates difference: the meticulously swept stoop next to the overgrown lot full of sunflowers, both forms of care.

I once spent a week walking the same three-mile loop in my city every evening, just to see what would change. Day one, I noticed nothing. Day two, the nothing got bored and started to dissolve. By day five, I knew which house had a cat that waited in the same window at 6:14, which fence post wobbled, where the jasmine bloomed so strongly it made you dizzy. I had not traveled anywhere, and yet I had arrived somewhere. Repetition, done with attention, becomes revelation.

Anthropologists call this “deep mapping” — learning a place the way indigenous trackers or long-time mail carriers do, layer by layer. It stands in opposition to the tourist gaze, which wants novelty without intimacy. To walk the same path until it becomes inexhaustible is a quiet rebellion against a culture that tells you happiness is always elsewhere, newer, faster.

And if walking returns us to human scale, the night sky rescues us from it.

Go somewhere truly dark, if you can. Away from porch lights and gas stations. Let your eyes adapt for twenty minutes — that’s how long rhodopsin in your rods takes to fully recharge. Slowly, the sky fills in. First the bright anchors: Venus, Jupiter, Sirius. Then the Milky Way, that pale river of 100 to 400 billion stars, smudged across the black. Then, if you’re lucky and patient, a satellite gliding silently, and a meteor burning up in a second — a grain of dust from a comet ending its four-billion-year journey in your retina.

It’s a cliché to feel small under the stars, but the feeling deserves unpacking, because smallness can mean two opposite things. It can mean insignificance: I am nothing, nothing matters. Or it can mean belonging: I am part of something so vast and old and intricate that my aliveness is improbable and precious.

Consider the numbers. Light from the Andromeda Galaxy left 2.5 million years ago, before Homo sapiens existed, and is just now hitting your eye. The calcium in your bones, the iron in your blood, the oxygen you’re breathing were forged in the cores of massive stars that exploded. You are, in the most literal sense, stardust that woke up and started wondering about itself. Carl Sagan said that, and it’s become a poster, but sit with it until it stops being cute and starts being vertiginous.

Astronomy also teaches humility about time. Human civilization is about six thousand years old — a blink. The Earth is 4.5 billion years old. If you compress Earth’s history into a single calendar year, life appears in March, dinosaurs show up on Christmas Day and vanish the day after, and all of human history happens in the last fourteen seconds of New Year’s Eve. Every grudge, every empire, every love letter fits into those fourteen seconds.

Does that make our concerns meaningless? I think it does the opposite. It makes attention sacred. In an indifferent universe, care is the only meaning that isn’t borrowed. When you choose to comfort a crying child at 3 a.m., to really listen, to tend a garden you will never see mature, you are asserting value where physics offers none. That is not small. That is cosmic defiance.

This is why I love both microscopes and telescopes. Put a drop of pond water under a microscope and you see paramecia whirling, rotifers opening like umbrellas, an entire Serengeti in a bead. Point a telescope at a patch of sky that looks empty and the Hubble Deep Field reveals ten thousand galaxies. Bigness and smallness mirror each other. As the physicist Richard Feynman put it, there is “plenty of room at the bottom.” And plenty of room at the top, too.

So where does that leave us, you and I, here at the end of this long, winding walk that started with a blue mug?

It leaves us with practice, not conclusions. Freedom — real creative freedom, not just consumer choice — is a practice. It looks like this: protect your mornings when you can. Choose what you attend to, over and over, even when you fail. Drink water and remember you are water. Write things down by hand so they can collide later. Walk the same street until it surprises you. Look up.

And write, or draw, or sing, or cook, or build, or garden, freely, without immediately asking if it’s useful or marketable or good enough to post. The world will try to grade everything. Make something that is only for the joy of seeing what your mind does when no one is watching. That is what I tried to do here — not to impress, but to follow curiosity wherever it tugged.

If you’ve read this far, you’ve given me the rarest gift: your sustained attention for a few thousand words in a world that wants it in three-second bursts. Thank you. I hope you feel, as I do now, a little more awake, a little more porous, a little more connected to sparrows and stars and strangers.

Tomorrow morning, the light will come through the window again, a little different from today. The kettle will sing. The tide — out there, and in here — will have shifted. There will be another threshold to cross. Cross it slowly. Notice the steam. Listen for the argument on the fence. Then step outside and see what the world wants to show you when you finally, freely, look.
